lines: Notice how reasonable this setup sounds before anything goes wrong.
One leader, one place to read from, nothing about that description admits a second possibility.
The trap is exactly that the description stopped being true the moment the leader changed, and the client never found out.
Before you pick, think carefully about what order these two events actually happened in.
The write didn't just start earlier. It finished, entirely, before the read even began.
answer: Not linearizable, and the reasoning is stricter than it might feel.
Once a write has completed, any correct account of what happened has to place it before anything that starts afterward.
A read placed after that write is required to see the new value, and this one didn't, so there is no legal account of this history at all.

lines: Hold the two parts of this promise apart, because people usually remember only the first one.
Every operation gets to look like it happened all at once, somewhere inside its own interval.
But where inside that interval isn't free to choose. If one operation's answer came back before another even started, the first one's instant has to come first too.
This is worth sitting with longer than it first seems to deserve.
Checking one object on its own, in isolation, is enough. Nothing about the rest of the system has to be re-checked once every object passes that test individually.
And no operation that's still pending is ever allowed to hold up another one just to stay correct.
Watch what the checker is actually doing here, because it's a search, not a shortcut.
It tries orderings until it finds one that both respects what the data is allowed to do and respects the order things really happened in.
For a history that's already correct, that search barely has to try.
Now feed the exact same search the broken version, and watch it come back empty.
Every ordering it tries breaks one of the two rules or the other. Not most orderings. Every single one.
That emptiness isn't the checker failing to find an answer. It is the answer, stated as plainly as a proof can state it.
Before you accept the fix as free, look closely at what it's actually trading away.
Confirming a quorum before answering does remove the stale value, completely.

But under perfectly synchronized clocks that confirmation still costs a full round trip somewhere, and once clocks carry real uncertainty, every single operation pays something close to that uncertainty, with no way around it.
Carry forward the shape of the whole guarantee, not just its headline.
An instant for every operation, real time respected, checked one object at a time.
A stale leader's read has, formally, nowhere legal to go in that account. A quorum-confirmed one does.
And neither the guarantee nor the fix for violating it ever comes for free.
Before you answer, separate what a good track record actually tells you from what a guarantee has to cover.
A guarantee that holds for every possible history is a much stronger claim than a system that simply hasn't hit a bad one yet.
answer: No, and this is worth remembering past this one example.
Linearizability has to hold for every history the system could ever produce, not just the ones it happens to have produced so far.
A design missing the quorum check already contains the exact failure from the hook. The only thing missing is the partition that would reveal it.
